records.name: Cayley-Hamilton Theorem
records.statement: For a square complex matrix $A$, its characteristic polynomial satisfies $\chi_A(A)=0$.
records.scope: Mathlib proves the stronger theorem over arbitrary commutative rings. The alternative below proves the displayed complex case.
records.proofA:
Let $A\in M_n(R)$, with $R$ commutative, and set $C=XI-A$. In $M_n(R[X])$ the adjugate identity gives
\[\operatorname{adj}(C)C=\det(C)I=\chi_A(X)I.\]

Transfer this identity to $M_n(R)[X]$ and evaluate on the right at $A$. Although evaluation is not multiplicative in general, every right multiple of $XI-A$ evaluates to zero: $BA^{j+1}-BA^jA=0$ for each coefficient $B$. The left side therefore evaluates to zero, while the right side evaluates to $\chi_A(A)$. Thus $\chi_A(A)=0$.
records.proofB:
For $D=\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_n)$, one has $\chi_D(X)=\prod_i(X-\lambda_i)$ and hence $\chi_D(D)=0$. Similarity invariance gives the identity for every diagonalizable matrix.

Diagonalizable matrices are dense in $M_n(\mathbb C)$: triangularize $A$ and perturb its diagonal to have distinct entries. Since $A\mapsto\chi_A(A)$ is polynomial in the matrix entries, it is continuous. Passing to the limit proves $\chi_A(A)=0$ for every $A\in M_n(\mathbb C)$.

theorem aeval_self_charpoly (M : Matrix n n R) : aeval M M.charpoly = 0 := by
  -- We begin with the fact $χ_M(t) I = adjugate (t I - M) * (t I - M)$,
  -- as an identity in `Matrix n n R[X]`.
  have h : M.charpoly • (1 : Matrix n n R[X]) = adjugate (charmatrix M) * charmatrix M :=
    (adjugate_mul _).symm
  -- Using the algebra isomorphism `Matrix n n R[X] ≃ₐ[R] Polynomial (Matrix n n R)`,
  -- we have the same identity in `Polynomial (Matrix n n R)`.
  apply_fun matPolyEquiv at h
  simp only [map_mul, matPolyEquiv_charmatrix] at h
  -- Because the coefficient ring `Matrix n n R` is non-commutative,
  -- evaluation at `M` is not multiplicative.
  -- However, any polynomial which is a product of the form $N * (t I - M)$
  -- is sent to zero, because the evaluation function puts the polynomial variable
  -- to the right of any coefficients, so everything telescopes.
  apply_fun fun p => p.eval M at h
  rw [eval_mul_X_sub_C] at h
  -- Now $χ_M (t) I$, when thought of as a polynomial of matrices
  -- and evaluated at some `N` is exactly $χ_M (N)$.
  rw [matPolyEquiv_smul_one, eval_map] at h
  -- Thus we have $χ_M(M) = 0$, which is the desired result.
  exact h

records.name: Fundamental Theorem of Algebra
records.statement: Every nonconstant polynomial $P\in\mathbb C[X]$ has a complex root.
records.proofA:
Let $P\in\mathbb C[X]$ be nonconstant and suppose $P(z)\ne0$ for all $z$. Then $g=1/P$ is entire. The leading term of $P$ dominates at infinity, so $|P(z)|\to\infty$ and $g(z)\to0$ as $|z|\to\infty$.

Thus $g$ is bounded outside a disk and, by compactness, on the disk. Liouville's theorem makes $g$ constant; its limit at infinity forces $g=0$, contradicting $Pg=1$. Hence $P$ has a root.
records.proofB:
First let $P\in\mathbb R[X]$ have degree $n>0$. Induct on $v_2(n)$. If $n$ is odd, the intermediate value theorem gives a real root. Otherwise, write $z_1,\ldots,z_n$ for the roots in an algebraic closure of $\mathbb C$ and, for $t\in\mathbb R$, set
\[Q_t(Y)=\prod_{i<j}(Y-z_i-z_j-tz_i z_j).\]

The coefficients of $Q_t$ are symmetric in the $z_i$, hence real, and $v_2(\deg Q_t)=v_2(n)-1$. By induction, $Q_t$ has a complex root. Taking more parameters $t$ than pairs $(i,j)$ gives a pair for which $z_i+z_j+t z_i z_j$ is complex for two distinct values of $t$. Consequently $z_i+z_j,z_i z_j\in\mathbb C$. Both $z_i,z_j$ solve a quadratic over $\mathbb C$, whose roots lie in $\mathbb C$.

For $P\in\mathbb C[X]$ nonconstant, $P\overline P$ has real coefficients. A complex root of $P\overline P$ is either a root of $P$ or the conjugate of one.

  -- Thus `f = 0`, contradicting the fact that `0 < degree f`.

records.name: Infinitude of Primes
records.statement: There are infinitely many prime natural numbers.
records.proofA: Fix $N\in\mathbb N$ and let $p$ be a prime divisor of $N!+1$. If $p\le N$, then $p\mid N!$, so $p\mid(N!+1)-N!=1$, a contradiction. Therefore $p>N$. Since $N$ was arbitrary, there are infinitely many primes.
records.proofB:
Suppose the primes are $p_1,\ldots,p_r$. Unique factorization and geometric series yield
\[\sum_{n\ge1}\frac1n=\prod_{i=1}^{r}\left(1-\frac1{p_i}\right)^{-1}<\infty.\]
More explicitly, every finite harmonic sum is bounded by the product. This contradicts divergence of the harmonic series.

namespace Proofscape.RouteB

open Set Nat
open scoped BigOperators

/-- Reciprocal as a completely multiplicative function on natural numbers. -/
noncomputable def reciprocal : ℕ →* ℝ where
  toFun n := (n : ℝ)⁻¹
  map_one' := by simp
  map_mul' := by intro m n; simp [mul_comm]

/-- Euler's proof: a finite set of all primes would make the harmonic series
converge, since its terms form the geometric Euler product over that set. -/
theorem infinitely_many_primes_euler : {p : ℕ | p.Prime}.Infinite := by
  intro hfinite
  classical
  let S := hfinite.toFinset
  have hall : ∀ p : ℕ, p.Prime → p ∈ S := by
    intro p hp
    exact hfinite.mem_toFinset.mpr hp
  have hsmall : ∀ {p : ℕ}, p.Prime → ‖reciprocal p‖ < 1 := by
    intro p hp
    have hpR : (1 : ℝ) < p := by exact_mod_cast hp.one_lt
    have hpos : (0 : ℝ) < p := lt_trans zero_lt_one hpR
    change ‖(p : ℝ)⁻¹‖ < 1
    rw [Real.norm_eq_abs, abs_of_nonneg (le_of_lt (inv_pos.mpr hpos))]
    exact (inv_lt_one₀ hpos).mpr hpR
  obtain ⟨hsum, hproduct⟩ :=
    EulerProduct.summable_and_hasSum_factoredNumbers_prod_filter_prime_geometric hsmall S
  let e : ℕ → Nat.factoredNumbers S := fun n =>
    ⟨n + 1, Nat.mem_factoredNumbers_iff_forall_le.mpr
      ⟨Nat.succ_ne_zero n, fun p _ hp _ => hall p hp⟩⟩
  have hinj : Function.Injective e := by
    intro i j hij
    have h : i + 1 = j + 1 := congrArg Subtype.val hij
    omega
  have hs := hsum.comp_injective hinj
  have heval (n : ℕ) : ‖reciprocal (e n)‖ = (1 : ℝ) / (n + 1) := by
    change ‖(((n + 1 : ℕ) : ℝ)⁻¹)‖ = (1 : ℝ) / (n + 1)
    rw [Real.norm_eq_abs, abs_of_nonneg (by positivity), one_div]
    simp
  change Summable (fun n : ℕ => ‖reciprocal (e n)‖) at hs
  simp only [heval] at hs
  exact Real.not_summable_one_div_natCast ((summable_nat_add_iff 1).mp (by simpa using hs))

records.name: Pythagorean Theorem
records.statement: For perpendicular vectors $u,v$ in a real inner-product space, $\|u+v\|^2=\|u\|^2+\|v\|^2$; equivalently a right triangle with legs $a,b$ and hypotenuse $c$ satisfies $a^2+b^2=c^2$.
records.scope: Mathlib states the vector identity; the dissection uses a geometric translation to the triangle formulation.
records.proofA:
For $\langle u,v\rangle=0$, bilinearity gives
\[\|u+v\|^2=\langle u+v,u+v\rangle=\|u\|^2+2\langle u,v\rangle+\|v\|^2=\|u\|^2+\|v\|^2.\]
Taking $a=\|u\|$, $b=\|v\|$ and $c=\|u+v\|$ yields $a^2+b^2=c^2$.
records.proofB:
Arrange four copies of a right triangle with legs $a,b$ and hypotenuse $c$ inside a square of side $a+b$, leaving a central square of side $c$. The adjacent acute angles are complementary, so the central angles are right angles.

Area additivity gives $(a+b)^2=4(ab/2)+c^2$. Expanding and cancelling $2ab$ yields $a^2+b^2=c^2$.

records.name: Intermediate Value Theorem
records.statement: If $a\le b$, $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and $f(a)\le y\le f(b)$, then $f(c)=y$ for some $c\in[a,b]$. The reversed endpoint order is analogous.
records.proofA: The interval $[a,b]$ is connected, and its continuous image $f([a,b])\subseteq\mathbb R$ is connected. Every connected subset of $\mathbb R$ is an interval. Since $f(a),f(b)\in f([a,b])$ and $f(a)\le y\le f(b)$, we have $y\in f([a,b])$. Thus $y=f(c)$ for some $c\in[a,b]$.
records.proofB:
Endpoint equality gives the result immediately. Otherwise $f(a)<y<f(b)$. Put
\[S=\{x\in[a,b]:f(x)<y\},\qquad c=\sup S.\]
Then $S\ne\varnothing$, $S$ is bounded above, and $c\in[a,b]$.

If $f(c)<y$, continuity and $c<b$ give a point of $S$ to the right of $c$, contrary to $c$ being an upper bound. If $f(c)>y$, continuity and $c>a$ give an upper bound for $S$ strictly below $c$, contrary to the definition of $c$. Hence $f(c)=y$.

theorem intermediate_value_by_supremum {a b y : ℝ} {f : ℝ → ℝ}

    (hay : f a ≤ y) (hyb : y ≤ f b) :
    ∃ c ∈ Icc a b, f c = y := by

  · exact ⟨a, ⟨le_rfl, hab⟩, ha⟩
  by_cases hb : f b = y
  · exact ⟨b, ⟨hab, le_rfl⟩, hb⟩
  have hfa : f a < y := lt_of_le_of_ne hay ha
  have hfb : y < f b := lt_of_le_of_ne hyb (Ne.symm hb)
  let S : Set ℝ := {x | x ∈ Icc a b ∧ f x < y}
  have hne : S.Nonempty := ⟨a, ⟨⟨le_rfl, hab⟩, hfa⟩⟩
  have hbounded : BddAbove S := ⟨b, fun _ hx => hx.1.2⟩
  let c := sSup S
  have hca : a ≤ c := le_csSup hbounded ⟨⟨le_rfl, hab⟩, hfa⟩
  have hcb : c ≤ b := csSup_le hne (fun _ hx => hx.1.2)

    intro hcy
    have hcb' : c < b := by
      by_contra h
      have : c = b := le_antisymm hcb (le_of_not_gt h)
      rw [this] at hcy
      linarith
    obtain ⟨δ, hδ, hcont⟩ := (Metric.continuousOn_iff.mp hf) c hc (y - f c) (by linarith)
    let z := min b (c + δ / 2)
    have hcz : c < z := lt_min hcb' (by linarith)
    have hzb : z ≤ b := min_le_left _ _
    have hzbound : z ≤ c + δ / 2 := min_le_right _ _
    have hz : z ∈ Icc a b := ⟨le_trans hca (le_of_lt hcz), hzb⟩
    have hdist : dist z c < δ := by
      rw [Real.dist_eq, abs_of_nonneg (by linarith)]
      linarith
    have hdiff := hcont z hz hdist
    rw [Real.dist_eq, abs_lt] at hdiff
    have hzS : z ∈ S := ⟨hz, by linarith [hdiff.2]⟩
    have hzc : z ≤ c := le_csSup hbounded hzS
    linarith
  have hnot_gt : ¬ y < f c := by
    intro hyc
    have hac : a < c := by
      by_contra h
      have : c = a := le_antisymm (le_of_not_gt h) hca
      rw [this] at hyc
      linarith
    obtain ⟨δ, hδ, hcont⟩ := (Metric.continuousOn_iff.mp hf) c hc (f c - y) (by linarith)
    let z := max a (c - δ / 2)
    have hza : a ≤ z := le_max_left _ _
    have hzc : z < c := max_lt hac (by linarith)
    have hzbound : c - δ / 2 ≤ z := le_max_right _ _
    have hupper : ∀ t ∈ S, t ≤ z := by
      intro t ht
      by_contra htz
      have htz' : z < t := lt_of_not_ge htz
      have htc : t ≤ c := le_csSup hbounded ht
      have hdist : dist t c < δ := by
        rw [Real.dist_eq, abs_of_nonpos (by linarith)]
        linarith
      have hdiff := hcont t ht.1 hdist
      rw [Real.dist_eq, abs_lt] at hdiff
      linarith [hdiff.1, ht.2]
    have hcz : c ≤ z := csSup_le hne hupper
    linarith
  exact ⟨c, hc, le_antisymm (le_of_not_gt hnot_gt) (le_of_not_gt hnot_lt)⟩

records.name: Irrationality of $\sqrt{2}$
records.statement: $\sqrt 2$ is irrational.
records.scope: The alternative uses descent on positive integers. Its length interpretation is geometric, but the algebraic sketch does not require a geometry library.
records.proofA:
For $n\in\mathbb N$, $\sqrt n\in\mathbb Q$ if and only if $n$ is a square. Indeed, write $\sqrt n=a/b$ in lowest terms, with $b>0$. Then $n=a^2/b^2$; since $\gcd(a^2,b^2)=1$, the reduced denominator is $b^2=1$. Thus $n=a^2$. The converse is immediate.

The prime $2$ is irreducible and hence not a square: $2=m^2$ would force $m$ to be a unit. The criterion therefore gives $\sqrt2\notin\mathbb Q$.
records.proofB:
Suppose $b/a=\sqrt2$ for positive integers $a,b$, with $a$ minimal. Then $b^2=2a^2$ and $a<b<2a$. Set
\[a'=b-a,\qquad b'=2a-b.\]
Both are positive integers, $a'<a$, and
\[(b')^2-2(a')^2=(2a-b)^2-2(b-a)^2=2a^2-b^2=0.\]
Thus $b'/a'=\sqrt2$, contradicting the minimality of $a$.

import Mathlib.NumberTheory.Real.Irrational
import Mathlib.Tactic.Linarith
import Mathlib.Tactic.NormNum
import Mathlib.Tactic.FieldSimp

namespace Proofscape.RouteB

/-- A hypothetical solution descends from (a,b) to (b-a,2a-b). -/
theorem sqrt_two_descent (a : ℕ) :
    ∀ b : ℕ, 0 < a → b ^ 2 = 2 * a ^ 2 → False := by
  induction a using Nat.strong_induction_on with
  | ind a ih =>
    intro b ha h
    have hab : a < b := by nlinarith
    have hba : b < 2 * a := by nlinarith
    have hsub₁ : b - a + a = b := Nat.sub_add_cancel (by omega)
    have hsub₂ : 2 * a - b + b = 2 * a := Nat.sub_add_cancel (by omega)
    have hnew : (2 * a - b) ^ 2 = 2 * (b - a) ^ 2 := by nlinarith
    exact ih (b - a) (by omega) (2 * a - b) (by omega) hnew

/-- Irrationality of sqrt 2 by the geometric infinite descent. -/
theorem irrational_sqrt_two_by_descent : Irrational (Real.sqrt 2) := by
  rw [irrational_iff_ne_rational]
  intro a b hb h
  have hbR : (b : ℝ) ≠ 0 := by exact_mod_cast hb
  have hsqrt : (Real.sqrt 2) ^ 2 = (2 : ℝ) := Real.sq_sqrt (by norm_num)
  have hmul : Real.sqrt 2 * b = a := by
    rw [h]
    field_simp
  have heqR : (a : ℝ) ^ 2 = 2 * (b : ℝ) ^ 2 := by
    calc
      (a : ℝ) ^ 2 = (Real.sqrt 2 * b) ^ 2 := by rw [hmul]
      _ = 2 * (b : ℝ) ^ 2 := by rw [mul_pow, hsqrt]
  have heqZ : a ^ 2 = 2 * b ^ 2 := by exact_mod_cast heqR
  have heqN : a.natAbs ^ 2 = 2 * b.natAbs ^ 2 := by
    simpa [Int.natAbs_mul, Int.natAbs_pow] using congrArg Int.natAbs heqZ
  exact sqrt_two_descent b.natAbs a.natAbs (Int.natAbs_pos.mpr hb) heqN

end Proofscape.RouteB

records.name: Sylow's First Theorem
records.statement: If $G$ is finite, $p$ is prime and $p^k\mid |G|$, then $G$ has a subgroup of order $p^k$.
records.scope: The theorem displayed is the general p-power-divisor form; Wielandt’s sketch first proves the maximal p-power case.
records.proofA:
Begin with $H=\{1\}$, of order $p^0$. Suppose $|H|=p^j$ and $p^{j+1}\mid |G|$. In the action of $H$ on $G/H$, every nontrivial orbit has cardinal divisible by $p$, while the fixed cosets are identified with $N_G(H)/H$. Thus
\[|N_G(H)/H|\equiv |G/H|\equiv0\pmod p.\]

By Cauchy's theorem, $N_G(H)/H$ contains a subgroup of order $p$. Its inverse image in $N_G(H)$ contains $H$ and has order $p^{j+1}$. Iteration gives a subgroup of order $p^k$.
records.proofB:
Write $|G|=p^rm$, where $p\nmid m$. Let $G$ act on the subsets of $G$ of size $p^r$. The binomial congruence
\[\binom{p^rm}{p^r}\equiv m\not\equiv0\pmod p\]
implies that some orbit has size prime to $p$. For its stabilizer $H$, orbit–stabilizer gives $p^r\mid|H|$. If $x$ belongs to the stabilized subset, the free orbit $Hx$ lies in that subset; hence $|H|\le p^r$ and $|H|=p^r$.

A finite $p$-group of order $p^r$ has subgroups of order $p^j$ for $0\le j\le r$: take a central subgroup of order $p$, induct in the quotient, and lift by inverse images. Applying this to $H$ proves the general case.

records.name: Banach Fixed-Point Theorem
records.statement: Every contraction $f:X\to X$ on a nonempty complete metric space has a unique fixed point.
records.proofA:
Choose $x_0\in X$, put $x_n=f^n(x_0)$, and write $d_0=d(x_0,x_1)$. If $f$ is $q$-contracting, $0\le q<1$, then
\[d(x_n,x_{n+1})\le q^nd_0,\qquad d(x_n,x_m)\le \frac{q^nd_0}{1-q}\quad(m>n).\]
Thus $(x_n)$ is Cauchy and converges, by completeness, to some $x$. Continuity gives $f(x)=\lim_n x_{n+1}=x$. If $f(y)=y$, then $d(x,y)\le qd(x,y)$, so $x=y$.
records.proofB:
With $x_n=f^n(x_0)$ and $d_0=d(x_0,x_1)$, define
\[r_n=\frac{q^nd_0}{1-q},\qquad B_n=\overline B(x_n,r_n).\]
The inequality $d(x_n,x_{n+1})\le q^nd_0$ and the identity $q^nd_0+r_{n+1}=r_n$ give $B_{n+1}\subseteq B_n$. The $B_n$ are nonempty and closed, and $r_n\to0$.

Their centers form a Cauchy sequence; its limit $x$ belongs to every $B_n$ by closedness. Since $x_n\to x$, continuity yields $f(x)=x$. For any two fixed points $x,y$, $d(x,y)\le qd(x,y)$, hence $x=y$.

records.name: Fermat's Two Squares Theorem
records.statement: If $p$ is prime and $p\equiv1\pmod4$, then $p=a^2+b^2$ for some $a,b\in\mathbb N$.
records.proofA:
A rational prime $p$ is prime in $\mathbb Z[i]$ precisely when $p\equiv3\pmod4$. For $p\equiv1\pmod4$, write $p=zw$ in $\mathbb Z[i]$ with $z,w$ nonunits. The norm is multiplicative and $N(z),N(w)>1$; hence
\[N(z)N(w)=N(p)=p^2.\]
Primality of $p$ forces $N(z)=p$. Writing $z=a+bi$ gives $p=a^2+b^2$; replace $a,b$ by their absolute values.
records.proofB:
Write $p=4k+1$ and let $S$ be the finite set of positive triples satisfying $x^2+4yz=p$. Define
\[(x,y,z)\longmapsto\begin{cases}(x+2z,z,y-x-z),&x+z<y,\\(x-2y,x+z-y,y),&2y<x,\\(2y-x,y,x+z-y),&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}\]
The boundary $x+z=y$ would make $p=(x+2z)^2$, and $x=2y$ would make $4\mid p$; neither occurs. Direct verification now shows that the map preserves $S$ and is an involution. Its unique fixed point is $(1,1,k)$: the middle case gives $x=y$, and primality in $p=x(x+4z)$ gives $x=1$. Thus $|S|$ is odd.

The involution $(x,y,z)\mapsto(x,z,y)$ therefore has a fixed point $(x,y,y)$, yielding $p=x^2+(2y)^2$.

records.name: Lagrange's Subgroup Theorem
records.statement: If $H$ is a subgroup of a finite group $G$, then $|H|$ divides $|G|$.
records.proofA:
The left cosets of $H$ partition $G$, and $h\mapsto gh$ is a bijection $H\to gH$ for each $g\in G$. Hence
\[|G|=[G:H]|H|,\]
so $|H|\mid|G|$.
records.proofB: Let $H$ act on $G$ by left multiplication. If $hg=g$, cancellation gives $h=1$; thus each stabilizer is trivial. Orbit–stabilizer gives $|H\cdot g|=|H|$ for every $g$. The orbits partition $G$, so $|G|$ is a multiple of $|H|$.

import Mathlib.GroupTheory.GroupAction.CardCommute

namespace Proofscape.RouteB

open Finset

/-- Left multiplication by a subgroup is a free action. -/
theorem subgroup_stabilizer_trivial {G : Type*} [Group G] (H : Subgroup G) (g : G) :
    MulAction.stabilizer H g = ⊥ := by
  ext h
  simp only [MulAction.mem_stabilizer_iff, Subgroup.mem_bot]
  constructor
  · intro hh
    apply Subtype.ext
    change (h : G) = 1
    change (h : G) * g = g at hh
    have : (h : G) * g = 1 * g := by simpa only [one_mul] using hh
    exact mul_right_cancel this
  · intro hh
    subst h
    simp

/-- The orbits all have the order of H, so the orbit partition proves Lagrange. -/

    Fintype.card H ∣ Fintype.card G := by
  classical
  letI : Fintype (Quotient (MulAction.orbitRel H G)) := Fintype.ofFinite _
  rw [MulAction.card_eq_sum_card_group_div_card_stabilizer H G]
  apply Finset.dvd_sum
  intro orbit _
  have hs : Nat.card (MulAction.stabilizer H orbit.out) = 1 := by
    rw [subgroup_stabilizer_trivial H orbit.out]
    simp
  have hs' : Fintype.card (MulAction.stabilizer H orbit.out) = 1 := by
    simpa only [Nat.card_eq_fintype_card] using hs
  rw [hs', Nat.div_one]

records.name: Sum of first n integers: 1+…+n=n(n+1)/2
records.statement: For $n\in\mathbb N$, $1+2+\cdots+n=n(n+1)/2$.
records.proofA:
Set $N=n+1$ and $S=\sum_{i=0}^{N-1}i$. The index reversal $i\mapsto N-1-i$ gives
\[2S=\sum_{i=0}^{N-1}\bigl(i+(N-1-i)\bigr)=N(N-1)=n(n+1).\]
Consequently $S=n(n+1)/2$.
records.proofB:
For $n=0$ the formula is immediate. If $2\sum_{i=1}^{n}i=n(n+1)$, then
\[2\sum_{i=1}^{n+1}i=n(n+1)+2(n+1)=(n+1)(n+2).\]
The doubled identity follows by induction; division by $2$ gives the result.

records.name: Binomial theorem
records.statement: For $n\in\mathbb N$ and commuting elements $x,y$ of a semiring, $(x+y)^n=\sum_{k=0}^n\binom nk x^ky^{n-k}$.
records.proofA:
Induct on $n$. The case $n=0$ is immediate. Multiplying the induction hypothesis by $x+y$ and using $xy=yx$, the coefficient of $x^ky^{n+1-k}$ is
\[\binom n{k-1}+\binom nk=\binom{n+1}k\]
for $1\le k\le n$; the endpoint coefficients are $1$. This is the required expansion for $n+1$.
records.proofB:
Distributivity indexes the $2^n$ terms in $(x+y)^n$ by subsets $S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}$, choosing $x$ on $S$ and $y$ off $S$. If $|S|=k$, commutativity gives the term $x^ky^{n-k}$. There are $\binom nk$ such subsets, so grouping by $k$ gives
\[(x+y)^n=\sum_{k=0}^n\binom nk x^ky^{n-k}.\]

      ∑ s ∈ (univ : Finset (Fin n)).powerset, x ^ s.card * y ^ (n - s.card) := by
  simpa using (Finset.sum_pow_mul_eq_add_pow x y (univ : Finset (Fin n))).symm

/-- Group the subsets by cardinality; there are choose n k of size k. -/
theorem binomial_by_subsets {R : Type*} [CommSemiring R] (x y : R) (n : ℕ) :
    (x + y) ^ n = ∑ k ∈ range (n + 1), (n.choose k) • (x ^ k * y ^ (n - k)) := by
  rw [binomial_expand_subsets]
  rw [Finset.sum_powerset]
  simp only [Finset.card_univ, Fintype.card_fin]
  apply Finset.sum_congr rfl
  intro k hk
  simpa using (Finset.sum_powersetCard k (univ : Finset (Fin n))
    (fun j => x ^ j * y ^ (n - j)))

/-- Two commuting elements generate a commutative subsemiring; apply the
subset-counting proof there and map the result back to the original semiring. -/
theorem binomial_by_subsets_of_commute {R : Type*} [Semiring R] (x y : R)
    (hxy : Commute x y) (n : ℕ) :
    (x + y) ^ n = ∑ k ∈ range (n + 1), (n.choose k) • (x ^ k * y ^ (n - k)) := by
  classical
  let S := Subsemiring.closure ({x, y} : Set R)
  have hcomm : ({x, y} : Set R).Pairwise Commute := by
    intro a ha b hb hab
    simp only [Set.mem_insert_iff, Set.mem_singleton_iff] at ha hb
    rcases ha with rfl | rfl <;> rcases hb with rfl | rfl
    · exact Commute.refl _
    · exact hxy
    · exact hxy.symm
    · exact Commute.refl _
  letI : IsMulCommutative S := Subsemiring.isMulCommutative_closure hcomm
  let xx : S := ⟨x, Subsemiring.subset_closure (by simp)⟩
  let yy : S := ⟨y, Subsemiring.subset_closure (by simp)⟩
  have h := binomial_by_subsets xx yy n
  have h' := congrArg (fun z : S => (z : R)) h
  simpa using h'

records.name: There are irrational numbers / R is uncountable
records.statement: The real numbers are uncountable. Consequently, some real number is irrational.
records.proofA:
Every real is represented by a rational Cauchy sequence, so $|\mathbb R|\le|\mathbb Q^{\mathbb N}|=2^{\aleph_0}$. Conversely,
\[(b_j)_{j\ge1}\longmapsto\sum_{j\ge1}2b_j3^{-j},\qquad b_j\in\{0,1\},\]
is injective: at the first differing digit, the leading difference exceeds the sum of all later differences. Thus $|\mathbb R|=2^{\aleph_0}>\aleph_0$ by Cantor's theorem. Since $\mathbb Q$ is countable, $\mathbb R\setminus\mathbb Q\ne\varnothing$.
records.proofB:
Suppose $x_1,x_2,\ldots$ enumerates $\mathbb R$. Recursively choose nonempty closed intervals $I_n=[a_n,b_n]$ such that
\[I_n\subseteq I_{n-1},\quad b_n-a_n\le2^{-n},\quad x_n\notin I_n.\]
Let $x=\sup_n a_n$. Nestedness gives $a_n\le x\le b_n$ for every $n$, so $x\in I_n$ and $x\ne x_n$ for all $n$, a contradiction. Hence $\mathbb R$ is uncountable; countability of $\mathbb Q$ gives an irrational real.

records.name: Divergence of the harmonic series
records.statement: The harmonic series $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}1/n$ diverges.
records.scope: Infinitely many primes is a consequence, but infinitude alone does not assert divergence of the prime reciprocal series. The Euler equivalence is between the two divergence statements.
records.proofA:
Cauchy's condensation criterion states that, for $a_n\ge0$ nonincreasing,
\[\sum_{n\ge1}a_n<\infty\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\sum_{j\ge0}2^ja_{2^j}<\infty.\]
For $a_n=1/n$, every condensed term equals $1$. Thus the harmonic series is not summable; its nondecreasing partial sums tend to $+\infty$.
records.proofB:
Suppose $\sum_p1/p<\infty$ and choose $y$ with $\sum_{p>y}1/p<1/2$. At most $N\sum_{p>y}1/p<N/2$ integers $m\le N$ have a prime factor greater than $y$. Every remaining $m$ is a square times a squarefree product of primes at most $y$, giving at most $2^{\pi(y)}\sqrt N$ possibilities. For large $N$ this is $<N/2$, a contradiction. Thus $\sum_p1/p=\infty$, and the harmonic series diverges by comparison.

Conversely, unique factorization gives
\[H_N\le\prod_{p\le N}(1-p^{-1})^{-1},\qquad \log\prod_{p\le N}(1-p^{-1})^{-1}\le2\sum_{p\le N}\frac1p.\]
Harmonic divergence therefore forces divergence of the prime reciprocal series. The two divergence statements are equivalent.

open Set Nat

/-- Union bound for numbers with a prime factor above the threshold. -/
theorem rough_count_bound (N k : ℕ) :
    #(roughNumbersUpTo N k) ≤
      N * (N.succ.primesBelow \ k.primesBelow).sum (fun p ↦ (1 : ℝ) / p) := by
  simp_rw [Finset.mul_sum, mul_one_div]
  exact (Nat.cast_le.mpr <| roughNumbersUpTo_card_le N k).trans <|
    cast_sum (R := ℝ) .. ▸ Finset.sum_le_sum fun n _ ↦ cast_div_le

/-- Erdős's smooth/rough count gives a lower bound for every prime tail. -/
theorem prime_tail_lower_bound (k : ℕ) :
    1 / 2 ≤ ∑ p ∈ (4 ^ (#k.primesBelow + 1)).succ.primesBelow \ k.primesBelow,
      (1 / p : ℝ) := by
  set m : ℕ := 2 ^ #k.primesBelow
  set N₀ : ℕ := 2 * m ^ 2 with hN₀
  let S : ℝ := ((2 * N₀).succ.primesBelow \ k.primesBelow).sum (fun p ↦ (1 / p : ℝ))
  suffices 1 / 2 ≤ S by
    convert this using 5
    rw [show 4 = 2 ^ 2 by simp, pow_right_comm]
    ring
  suffices 2 * N₀ ≤ m * (2 * N₀).sqrt + 2 * N₀ * S by
    rwa [hN₀, ← mul_assoc, ← pow_two 2, ← mul_pow, sqrt_eq', ← sub_le_iff_le_add',
      cast_mul, cast_mul, cast_pow, cast_two,
      show (2 * (2 * m ^ 2) - m * (2 * m) : ℝ) = 2 * (2 * m ^ 2) * (1 / 2) by ring,
      mul_le_mul_iff_right₀ <| by positivity] at this
  calc (2 * N₀ : ℝ)
    _ = #((2 * N₀).smoothNumbersUpTo k) + #((2 * N₀).roughNumbersUpTo k) := by
        exact mod_cast ((2 * N₀).smoothNumbersUpTo_card_add_roughNumbersUpTo_card k).symm
    _ ≤ m * (2 * N₀).sqrt + #((2 * N₀).roughNumbersUpTo k) := by
        exact mod_cast Nat.add_le_add_right ((2 * N₀).smoothNumbersUpTo_card_le k) _
    _ ≤ m * (2 * N₀).sqrt + 2 * N₀ * S := by grw [rough_count_bound]; norm_cast

/-- If the harmonic series converged, its prime subseries would have small tails,
contradicting the smooth/rough counting bound. -/
theorem harmonic_diverges_by_erdos :
    ¬ Summable (fun n : ℕ => 1 / ((n + 1 : ℕ) : ℝ)) := by
  intro h
  have hall : Summable (fun n : ℕ => (1 : ℝ) / n) := by
    apply (summable_nat_add_iff (f := fun n : ℕ => (1 : ℝ) / n) 1).mp
    simpa using h
  have hp : Summable (indicator {p : ℕ | p.Prime} (fun n : ℕ ↦ (1 : ℝ) / n)) :=
    hall.indicator _
  obtain ⟨k, hk⟩ := hp.nat_tsum_vanishing (Iio_mem_nhds one_half_pos : Iio (1 / 2 : ℝ) ∈ 𝓝 0)
  specialize hk ({p | Nat.Prime p} ∩ {p | k ≤ p}) inter_subset_right
  rw [tsum_subtype, indicator_indicator,
    inter_eq_left.mpr fun n (hn : n ∈ {p | Nat.Prime p} ∩ {p | k ≤ p}) ↦ hn.1, mem_Iio] at hk
  have ht : Summable (indicator ({p | Nat.Prime p} ∩ {p | k ≤ p}) fun n ↦ (1 : ℝ) / n) := by
    convert hp.indicator {n : ℕ | k ≤ n} using 1
    simp only [indicator_indicator, inter_comm]
  refine ((prime_tail_lower_bound k).trans_lt <| LE.le.trans_lt ?_ hk).false
  convert! Summable.sum_le_tsum (primesBelow ((4 ^ (#k.primesBelow + 1)).succ) \ primesBelow k)
      (fun n _ ↦ indicator_nonneg (fun p _ ↦ by positivity) _) ht using 2 with p hp
  obtain ⟨hp₁, hp₂⟩ := mem_ofPred_eq ▸ Finset.mem_sdiff.mp hp
  have hpp := prime_of_mem_primesBelow hp₁
  refine (indicator_of_mem ?_ fun n : ℕ ↦ (1 / n : ℝ)).symm
  exact ⟨hpp, by simpa [primesBelow, hpp] using hp₂⟩

records.name: Cauchy's theorem for finite groups
records.statement: If prime $p$ divides the order of a finite group $G$, then $G$ has an element of order $p$.
records.proofA:
Let $T=\{(g_1,\ldots,g_p)\in G^p:g_1\cdots g_p=1\}$. The first $p-1$ entries determine the last, so $|T|=|G|^{p-1}\equiv0\pmod p$. Cyclic rotation acts on $T$, with orbits of size $1$ or $p$. Hence the number of fixed points is divisible by $p$.

The identity tuple is fixed, so another fixed tuple exists. It is constant, $(g,\ldots,g)$, with $g\ne1$ and $g^p=1$. Since $p$ is prime, $\operatorname{ord}(g)=p$.
records.proofB:
Induct on $|G|$, using Cauchy's theorem for finite abelian groups. If a noncentral element $x$ has $p\mid|C_G(x)|$, induction applied to the proper centralizer gives the result. Otherwise every noncentral conjugacy class has size $[G:C_G(x)]$ divisible by $p$. The class equation then gives $p\mid|Z(G)|$, and the abelian case applied to $Z(G)$ finishes.

For the abelian case, induct on $|G|$ and choose $a\ne1$. If $p\mid\operatorname{ord}(a)$, a power of $a$ has order $p$. Otherwise $p\mid|G/\langle a\rangle|$; induction gives a quotient element of order $p$. A lift has order divisible by $p$, and an appropriate power has order $p$.

records.name: Quadratic reciprocity
records.statement: For distinct odd primes \(p,q\), \(\left(\frac pq\right)\left(\frac qp\right)=(-1)^{\frac{p-1}{2}\frac{q-1}{2}}\), where \(\left(\frac{\cdot}{\cdot}\right)\) is the Legendre symbol.
records.proofA:
Let $\chi_p,\chi_q$ be the quadratic characters for distinct odd primes $p,q$. In a field of characteristic $q$ containing a primitive $p$th root $\zeta$, set
\[\tau=\sum_{a\in\mathbb F_p^\times}\chi_p(a)\zeta^a.\]
Expanding $\tau\bar\tau$ and using $\sum_a\chi_p(a)=0$ gives $\tau\bar\tau=p$, while $\bar\tau=\chi_p(-1)\tau$. Hence $\tau^2=\chi_p(-1)p\ne0$.

Frobenius gives $\tau^q=\chi_p(q)\tau$. Euler's criterion in characteristic $q$ therefore yields
\[\chi_p(q)=\tau^{q-1}=(\chi_p(-1)p)^{(q-1)/2}
=(-1)^{((p-1)/2)((q-1)/2)}\chi_q(p).\]
Multiplication by $\chi_q(p)$ proves quadratic reciprocity.
records.proofB:
Put $a=(p-1)/2$ and $b=(q-1)/2$. Eisenstein's form of Gauss's lemma gives
\[\left(\frac qp\right)=(-1)^A,\quad A=\sum_{x=1}^{a}\left\lfloor\frac{qx}{p}\right\rfloor,\qquad
\left(\frac pq\right)=(-1)^B,\quad B=\sum_{y=1}^{b}\left\lfloor\frac{py}{q}\right\rfloor.\]

No lattice point in $1\le x\le a$, $1\le y\le b$ lies on $py=qx$. The lattice points on the two sides of this line are counted by $A$ and $B$, respectively. Thus $A+B=ab$, and the product of the two symbols is $(-1)^{ab}$.

import Mathlib.NumberTheory.LegendreSymbol.GaussEisensteinLemmas

namespace Proofscape.RouteB

open Finset

/-- Eisenstein's form of Gauss's lemma and the lattice-point count prove
quadratic reciprocity for distinct odd primes. -/
theorem quadratic_reciprocity_by_lattice {p q : ℕ} [Fact p.Prime] [Fact q.Prime]
    (hp : p ≠ 2) (hq : q ≠ 2) (hpq : p ≠ q) :
    legendreSym p q * legendreSym q p = (-1) ^ (p / 2 * (q / 2)) := by
  have hpOdd : p % 2 = 1 := (Nat.Prime.mod_two_eq_one_iff_ne_two Fact.out).mpr hp
  have hqOdd : q % 2 = 1 := (Nat.Prime.mod_two_eq_one_iff_ne_two Fact.out).mpr hq
  have hqp : (q : ZMod p) ≠ 0 := ZMod.prime_ne_zero p q hpq
  have hpq' : (p : ZMod q) ≠ 0 := ZMod.prime_ne_zero q p hpq.symm
  have h₁ := ZMod.eisenstein_lemma hp hqOdd hqp
  have h₂ := ZMod.eisenstein_lemma hq hpOdd hpq'
  have hcount := ZMod.sum_mul_div_add_sum_mul_div_eq_mul p q hqp
  rw [h₁, h₂, ← pow_add, hcount]

end Proofscape.RouteB

records.name: Newton identities
records.statement: For elementary symmetric polynomials $e_k$ and power sums $p_j=\sum_i x_i^j$, $ke_k=\sum_{j=1}^k(-1)^{j-1}e_{k-j}p_j$, with $e_0=1$.
records.proofA:
Fix $k>0$. Consider pairs $(S,i)$ with $|S|\le k$ and $i\in S$ when $|S|=k$, weighted by
\[w(S,i)=(-1)^{|S|}\left(\prod_{j\in S}x_j\right)x_i^{k-|S|}.\]
Toggling $i\in S$ is a fixed-point-free involution on these pairs; it preserves the monomial and reverses its sign. Thus $\sum w(S,i)=0$.

The terms with $|S|=k$ sum to $(-1)^kke_k$; those with $|S|=r<k$ sum to $(-1)^re_rp_{k-r}$. Rearrangement gives
\[ke_k=\sum_{j=1}^k(-1)^{j-1}e_{k-j}p_j.\]
For $k=0$ both sides vanish.
records.proofB:
In the formal power-series ring, let
\[E(t)=\prod_i(1+x_it)=\sum_{k\ge0}e_kt^k.\]
Its constant coefficient is $1$, so $E$ is invertible. Formal differentiation and geometric expansion give
\[\frac{tE'(t)}{E(t)}=\sum_i\frac{x_it}{1+x_it}
=\sum_{j\ge1}(-1)^{j-1}p_jt^j.\]
Multiply by $E(t)$ and compare coefficients of $t^k$. No division by $k$ occurs, so the identity holds over a commutative ring.

records.proofA:
Finite variance implies integrability. The strong law gives $\overline X_n\to\mu$ almost surely. For $\varepsilon>0$, the indicators $1_{\{|\overline X_n-\mu|>\varepsilon\}}$ converge almost surely to $0$ and are bounded by $1$. Dominated convergence therefore gives
\[\mathbb P(|\overline X_n-\mu|>\varepsilon)\longrightarrow0.\]
This is convergence in probability. Mathlib supplies the strong law and the almost-everywhere-to-in-measure implication separately.
records.proofB:
Let $\phi(t)=\mathbb E(e^{itX_1})$. Integrability and dominated convergence give $\phi(t)=1+i\mu t+o(t)$ as $t\to0$. By independence,
\[\phi_{\overline X_n}(t)=\phi(t/n)^n\longrightarrow e^{i\mu t}.\]
Lévy's continuity theorem gives $\overline X_n\Rightarrow\mu$. For $\varepsilon>0$, portmanteau applied to the closed set $\{x:|x-\mu|\ge\varepsilon\}$ gives
\[\limsup_n\mathbb P(|\overline X_n-\mu|\ge\varepsilon)\le0.\]
Hence $\overline X_n\to\mu$ in probability.

theorem strong_law_aux1 {c : ℝ} (c_one : 1 < c) {ε : ℝ} (εpos : 0 < ε) : ∀ᵐ ω, ∀ᶠ n : ℕ in atTop,
    |∑ i ∈ range ⌊c ^ n⌋₊, truncation (X i) i ω - 𝔼[∑ i ∈ range ⌊c ^ n⌋₊, truncation (X i) i]| <
    ε * ⌊c ^ n⌋₊ := by
  /- Let `S n = ∑ i ∈ range n, Y i` where `Y i = truncation (X i) i`. We should show that
    `|S k - 𝔼[S k]| / k ≤ ε` along the sequence of powers of `c`. For this, we apply Borel-Cantelli:
    it suffices to show that the converse probabilities are summable. From Chebyshev inequality,
    this will follow from a variance control `∑' Var[S (c^i)] / (c^i)^2 < ∞`. This is checked in
    `I2` using pairwise independence to expand the variance of the sum as the sum of the variances,
    and then a straightforward but tedious computation (essentially boiling down to the fact that
    the sum of `1/(c ^ i)^2` beyond a threshold `j` is comparable to `1/j^2`).
    Note that we have written `c^i` in the above proof sketch, but rigorously one should put integer
    parts everywhere, making things more painful. We write `u i = ⌊c^i⌋₊` for brevity. -/
  have c_pos : 0 < c := zero_lt_one.trans c_one
  have hX : ∀ i, AEStronglyMeasurable (X i) ℙ := fun i =>
    (hident i).symm.aestronglyMeasurable_snd hint.1
  have A : ∀ i, StronglyMeasurable (indicator (Set.Ioc (-i : ℝ) i) id) := fun i =>
    stronglyMeasurable_id.indicator measurableSet_Ioc
  set Y := fun n : ℕ => truncation (X n) n
  set S := fun n => ∑ i ∈ range n, Y i with hS
  let u : ℕ → ℕ := fun n => ⌊c ^ n⌋₊
  have u_mono : Monotone u := fun i j hij => Nat.floor_mono (pow_right_mono₀ c_one.le hij)
  have I1 : ∀ K, ∑ j ∈ range K, ((j : ℝ) ^ 2)⁻¹ * Var[Y j] ≤ 2 * 𝔼[X 0] := by
    intro K
    calc
      ∑ j ∈ range K, ((j : ℝ) ^ 2)⁻¹ * Var[Y j] ≤
          ∑ j ∈ range K, ((j : ℝ) ^ 2)⁻¹ * 𝔼[truncation (X 0) j ^ 2] := by
        gcongr with j
        rw [(hident j).truncation.variance_eq]
        exact variance_le_expectation_sq (hX 0).truncation
      _ ≤ 2 * 𝔼[X 0] := sum_variance_truncation_le hint (hnonneg 0) K
  let C := c ^ 5 * (c - 1)⁻¹ ^ 3 * (2 * 𝔼[X 0])
  have I2 : ∀ N, ∑ i ∈ range N, ((u i : ℝ) ^ 2)⁻¹ * Var[S (u i)] ≤ C := by
    intro N
    calc
      ∑ i ∈ range N, ((u i : ℝ) ^ 2)⁻¹ * Var[S (u i)] =
          ∑ i ∈ range N, ((u i : ℝ) ^ 2)⁻¹ * ∑ j ∈ range (u i), Var[Y j] := by
        congr 1 with i
        congr 1
        rw [hS, IndepFun.variance_sum]
        · intro j _
          exact (hident j).aestronglyMeasurable_fst.memLp_truncation
        · intro k _ l _ hkl
          exact (hindep hkl).comp (A k).measurable (A l).measurable
      _ = ∑ j ∈ range (u (N - 1)), (∑ i ∈ range N with j < u i, ((u i : ℝ) ^ 2)⁻¹) * Var[Y j] := by
        simp_rw [mul_sum, sum_mul, sum_sigma']
        refine sum_nbij' (fun p ↦ ⟨p.2, p.1⟩) (fun p ↦ ⟨p.2, p.1⟩) ?_ ?_ ?_ ?_ ?_
        · simp only [mem_sigma, mem_range, mem_filter, and_imp,
            Sigma.forall]
          exact fun a b haN hb ↦ ⟨hb.trans_le <| u_mono <| Nat.le_pred_of_lt haN, haN, hb⟩
        all_goals simp
      _ ≤ ∑ j ∈ range (u (N - 1)), c ^ 5 * (c - 1)⁻¹ ^ 3 / ↑j ^ 2 * Var[Y j] := by
        gcongr ∑ _ ∈ _, ?_ with j
        rcases eq_zero_or_pos j with (rfl | hj)
        · simp only [Nat.cast_zero]
          simp only [Y, Nat.cast_zero, truncation_zero, variance_zero, mul_zero, le_rfl]
        apply mul_le_mul_of_nonneg_right _ (variance_nonneg _ _)
        convert! sum_div_nat_floor_pow_sq_le_div_sq N (Nat.cast_pos.2 hj) c_one using 2
        · simp only [u, Nat.cast_lt]
        · simp only [u, one_div]
      _ = c ^ 5 * (c - 1)⁻¹ ^ 3 * ∑ j ∈ range (u (N - 1)), ((j : ℝ) ^ 2)⁻¹ * Var[Y j] := by
        simp_rw [mul_sum, div_eq_mul_inv, mul_assoc]
      _ ≤ c ^ 5 * (c - 1)⁻¹ ^ 3 * (2 * 𝔼[X 0]) := by
        apply mul_le_mul_of_nonneg_left (I1 _)

        exact pow_nonneg (inv_nonneg.2 (sub_nonneg.2 c_one.le)) _

      ENNReal.ofReal (ε⁻¹ ^ 2 * C) := by
    intro N
    calc
      ∑ i ∈ range N, ℙ {ω | (u i * ε : ℝ) ≤ |S (u i) ω - 𝔼[S (u i)]|} ≤
          ∑ i ∈ range N, ENNReal.ofReal (Var[S (u i)] / (u i * ε) ^ 2) := by

        apply meas_ge_le_variance_div_sq
        · exact memLp_finsetSum' _ fun j _ => (hident j).aestronglyMeasurable_fst.memLp_truncation
        · apply mul_pos (Nat.cast_pos.2 _) εpos
          refine zero_lt_one.trans_le ?_
          apply Nat.le_floor
          rw [Nat.cast_one]
          apply one_le_pow₀ c_one.le
      _ = ENNReal.ofReal (∑ i ∈ range N, Var[S (u i)] / (u i * ε) ^ 2) := by
        rw [ENNReal.ofReal_sum_of_nonneg fun i _ => ?_]
        exact div_nonneg (variance_nonneg _ _) (sq_nonneg _)
      _ ≤ ENNReal.ofReal (ε⁻¹ ^ 2 * C) := by
        apply ENNReal.ofReal_le_ofReal
        simp_rw [div_eq_inv_mul, ← inv_pow, mul_inv, mul_comm _ (ε⁻¹), mul_pow, mul_assoc,
          ← mul_sum]
        gcongr
        simpa only [inv_pow] using I2 N
  have I4 : (∑' i, ℙ {ω | (u i * ε : ℝ) ≤ |S (u i) ω - 𝔼[S (u i)]|}) < ∞ :=
    (le_of_tendsto_of_tendsto' (ENNReal.tendsto_nat_tsum _) tendsto_const_nhds I3).trans_lt
      ENNReal.ofReal_lt_top
  filter_upwards [ae_eventually_notMem I4.ne] with ω hω
  simp_rw [S, not_le, mul_comm, Finset.sum_apply] at hω
  convert! hω; simp only [Y, u, Finset.sum_apply]

theorem strong_law_ae_real {Ω : Type*} {m : MeasurableSpace Ω} {μ : Measure Ω}
    (X : ℕ → Ω → ℝ) (hint : Integrable (X 0) μ)
    (hindep : Pairwise ((· ⟂ᵢ[μ] ·) on X))
    (hident : ∀ i, IdentDistrib (X i) (X 0) μ μ) :
    ∀ᵐ ω ∂μ, Tendsto (fun n : ℕ => (∑ i ∈ range n, X i ω) / n) atTop (𝓝 μ[X 0]) := by
  let mΩ : MeasureSpace Ω := ⟨μ⟩
  -- first get rid of the trivial case where the space is not a probability space
  by_cases h : ∀ᵐ ω, X 0 ω = 0
  · have I : ∀ᵐ ω, ∀ i, X i ω = 0 := by
      rw [ae_all_iff]
      intro i
      exact (hident i).symm.ae_snd (p := fun x ↦ x = 0) measurableSet_eq h
    filter_upwards [I] with ω hω
    simpa [hω] using! (integral_eq_zero_of_ae h).symm
  have : IsProbabilityMeasure μ :=
    hint.isProbabilityMeasure_of_indepFun (X 0) (X 1) h (hindep zero_ne_one)
  -- then consider separately the positive and the negative part, and apply the result
  -- for nonnegative functions to them.
  let pos : ℝ → ℝ := fun x => max x 0
  let neg : ℝ → ℝ := fun x => max (-x) 0
  have posm : Measurable pos := measurable_id'.max measurable_const
  have negm : Measurable neg := measurable_id'.neg.max measurable_const
  have A : ∀ᵐ ω, Tendsto (fun n : ℕ => (∑ i ∈ range n, (pos ∘ X i) ω) / n) atTop (𝓝 𝔼[pos ∘ X 0]) :=
    strong_law_aux7 _ hint.pos_part (fun i j hij => (hindep hij).comp posm posm)
      (fun i => (hident i).comp posm) fun i ω => le_max_right _ _
  have B : ∀ᵐ ω, Tendsto (fun n : ℕ => (∑ i ∈ range n, (neg ∘ X i) ω) / n) atTop (𝓝 𝔼[neg ∘ X 0]) :=
    strong_law_aux7 _ hint.neg_part (fun i j hij => (hindep hij).comp negm negm)
      (fun i => (hident i).comp negm) fun i ω => le_max_right _ _
  filter_upwards [A, B] with ω hωpos hωneg
  convert! hωpos.sub hωneg using 2
  · simp only [pos, neg, ← sub_div, ← sum_sub_distrib, max_zero_sub_max_neg_zero_eq_self,
      Function.comp_apply]
  · simp +instances only [pos, neg, ← integral_sub hint.pos_part hint.neg_part,
      max_zero_sub_max_neg_zero_eq_self, Function.comp_apply, mΩ]

records.name: Central limit theorem (classical iid finite variance)
records.statement: For iid random variables with mean \(\mu\) and finite positive variance \(\sigma^2\), \(\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n}X_i-n\mu}{\sigma\sqrt{n}}\) converges in distribution to the standard normal law.
records.scope: Mathlib proves convergence to a Gaussian with the original variance; division by the positive standard deviation yields the displayed standard-normal form. The alternative uses truncation, moment determinacy and tightness.
records.proofA:
Set $Y_i=(X_i-\mu)/\sigma$. Then $\mathbb EY_i=0$, $\mathbb EY_i^2=1$, and the characteristic function satisfies $\phi(t)=1-t^2/2+o(t^2)$. Independence yields
\[\phi_{n^{-1/2}\sum_{i=1}^nY_i}(t)=\phi(t/\sqrt n)^n\longrightarrow e^{-t^2/2}.\]
The limit is the characteristic function of $N(0,1)$, so Lévy's continuity theorem gives the result. Mathlib first proves convergence to a Gaussian with the original variance and then rescales.
records.proofB:
Center $X_i$ and fix $M>0$. Write $X_i-\mu=Y_i^{(M)}+R_i^{(M)}$, where $Y_i^{(M)}$ is centered and truncated at $M$. Then $\operatorname{Var}(R_i^{(M)})\to0$, and independence gives
\[\operatorname{Var}\!\left(n^{-1/2}\sum_{i=1}^nR_i^{(M)}\right)=\operatorname{Var}(R_1^{(M)})\longrightarrow0\quad(M\to\infty)\]
uniformly in $n$.

For fixed $M$, expand each moment of $n^{-1/2}\sum_iY_i^{(M)}$. Singleton indices contribute $0$; only pairings survive in the limit. Thus the limiting moments are the Gaussian moments. Second-moment bounds give tightness, and Gaussian moment determinacy gives convergence to $N(0,\operatorname{Var}(Y_1^{(M)}))$. Chebyshev's inequality removes the remainder uniformly in $n$; letting $M\to\infty$ and dividing by $\sigma$ gives $N(0,1)$.

records.name: Liouville's theorem
records.statement: Every bounded entire function $f:\mathbb C\to\mathbb C$ is constant.
records.proofA:
If $|f|\le M$, Cauchy's derivative estimate gives, for every $z\in\mathbb C$ and $R>0$,
\[|f'(z)|\le \frac{M}{R}.\]
Letting $R\to\infty$ gives $f'=0$. Since $\mathbb C$ is connected, $f$ is constant.
records.proofB:
Write $f=u+iv$, where $u,v$ are bounded harmonic functions. The mean-value property gives
\[u(x)-u(y)=\frac1{\pi R^2}\left(\int_{D(x,R)}u-\int_{D(y,R)}u\right).\]
The symmetric difference of the disks has area $O(R|x-y|+|x-y|^2)$, so $|u(x)-u(y)|\to0$ as $R\to\infty$. Thus $u(x)=u(y)$; the same argument applies to $v$. Therefore $f$ is constant.

records.name: Nullstellensatz
records.statement: For an algebraically closed field $k$ and an ideal $I\subseteq k[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$, the ideal of polynomials vanishing on $V(I)$ is $\sqrt I$.
records.scope: Both sketches now prove the strong theorem. The alternate depends on the weak theorem, which must be supplied independently.
records.proofA:
If $f\in\sqrt I$, then $f^m\in I$ for some $m$, so $f$ vanishes on $V(I)$. Conversely, $R=k[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$ is Jacobson and
\[\sqrt I=\bigcap_{\substack{\mathfrak m\supseteq I\\\mathfrak m\text{ maximal}}}\mathfrak m.\]
Every maximal ideal is the vanishing ideal of a point of $k^n$. If $f$ vanishes on $V(I)$, it lies in each maximal ideal containing $I$, and hence in $\sqrt I$.
records.proofB:
Let $f\in I(V(I))$ and put $J=(I,1-tf)\subseteq k[x_1,\ldots,x_n,t]$. A common zero of $I$ has $f=0$, so $V(J)=\varnothing$. By the weak Nullstellensatz, $J$ is the unit ideal. Thus, for finitely many $g_j\in I$,
\[1=\sum_j a_j(x,t)g_j(x)+b(x,t)(1-tf(x)).\]
Substitute $t=f^{-1}$ in $R[f^{-1}]$ and clear a power of $f$: $f^m\in I$ for some $m$. Hence $f\in\sqrt I$. The reverse inclusion follows by evaluating $f^m\in I$ at points of $V(I)$.

records.name: Stirling's formula n! ~ √(2πn)(n/e)^n
records.statement: As \(n\to\infty\), \(n!\sim\sqrt{2\pi n}\,(n/e)^n\).
records.proofA:
Set $a_n=n!e^n/(n^n\sqrt n)$. Then
\[\log a_{n+1}-\log a_n=1-\left(n+\tfrac12\right)\log(1+1/n)=O(n^{-2}).\]
Thus $a_n\to L>0$. Wallis' product gives $\binom{2n}{n}\sim4^n/\sqrt{\pi n}$, and
\[\frac{a_n^2}{a_{2n}}=\frac{4^n\sqrt{2/n}}{\binom{2n}{n}}\longrightarrow\sqrt{2\pi}.\]
The left side tends to $L$, so $L=\sqrt{2\pi}$ and $n!\sim\sqrt{2\pi n}(n/e)^n$.
records.proofB:
Repeated integration by parts gives $n!=\int_0^\infty x^ne^{-x}\,dx$. With $x=n+\sqrt n\,u$,
\[n!=n^ne^{-n}\sqrt n\int_{-\sqrt n}^{\infty}
\exp\!\left(n\log(1+u/\sqrt n)-\sqrt n\,u\right)\,du.\]
For fixed $u$, the exponent tends to $-u^2/2$. The bound $\log(1+t)-t\le-c\min(t^2,|t|)$ for $t>-1$ gives an integrable dominating function $e^{-c\min(u^2,|u|)}$, uniformly in $n$. Dominated convergence and the Gaussian integral give the limiting integral $\sqrt{2\pi}$, proving the formula.

records.name: Cyclotomic polynomial Φₙ(x) is irreducible over Q
records.statement: For every integer $n\ge1$, the cyclotomic polynomial $\Phi_n(X)$ is irreducible over $\mathbb Q$.
records.proofA:
Let $\zeta$ be a primitive $n$th root and $f$ its monic minimal polynomial over $\mathbb Z$. Mathlib's key modular argument shows that, for every prime $p\nmid n$, $\zeta^p$ has the same minimal polynomial as $\zeta$: reduction modulo $p$ and Frobenius would otherwise force a repeated factor of $X^n-1$, contrary to its squarefreeness. Iterating over prime factors shows that every $\zeta^m$ with $(m,n)=1$ is a root of $f$.

Consequently $\deg f\ge\varphi(n)$. Since $f\mid\Phi_n$, both are monic, and $\deg\Phi_n=\varphi(n)$, we obtain $f=\Phi_n$. The fraction-field criterion gives irreducibility over $\mathbb Q$. For $n=1$, the result is immediate.
records.proofB:
Let $n>1$, let $\zeta$ be primitive of order $n$, and let $f\in\mathbb Z[X]$ be its monic irreducible factor of $X^n-1$. Fix a prime $p\nmid n$ and suppose $f(\zeta^p)\ne0$. As a product of differences of distinct $n$th roots, $f(\zeta^p)$ divides the discriminant $\pm n^n$ in the algebraic integers. But Frobenius gives
\[f(\zeta^p)\equiv f(\zeta)^p=0\pmod p.\]
It follows that $p\mid n^n$ in the algebraic integers, hence in $\mathbb Z$, a contradiction. Therefore $f(\zeta^p)=0$.

Iterating over prime factors shows that all primitive $n$th roots are roots of $f$. Since $f\mid\Phi_n$ and $\deg\Phi_n=\varphi(n)$, monicity and the root count give $f=\Phi_n$. Gauss's lemma gives irreducibility over $\mathbb Q$. The case $n=1$ is immediate.

    eval (ζ^p) f = 0 := by
  by_contra h
  -- eval (ζ^p) f divides disc(X^n-1)=±n^n in the algebraic integers
  -- Frobenius congruence makes it divisible by p; contract to ℤ for a contradiction
  sorry
theorem alternative : Irreducible (cyclotomic n ℚ) := by
  -- iterate prime_power_invariant; all φ(n) primitive roots are roots of f;
  -- compare degrees and use Gauss's lemma

theorem minpoly_eq_pow {p : ℕ} [hprime : Fact p.Prime] (hdiv : ¬p ∣ n) :
    minpoly ℤ μ = minpoly ℤ (μ ^ p) := by
  by_cases hn : n = 0
  · simp_all
  have hpos := Nat.pos_of_ne_zero hn
  by_contra hdiff
  set P := minpoly ℤ μ
  set Q := minpoly ℤ (μ ^ p)
  have Pmonic : P.Monic := minpoly.monic (h.isIntegral hpos)
  have Qmonic : Q.Monic := minpoly.monic ((h.pow_of_prime hprime.1 hdiv).isIntegral hpos)
  have Pirr : Irreducible P := minpoly.irreducible (h.isIntegral hpos)
  have Qirr : Irreducible Q := minpoly.irreducible ((h.pow_of_prime hprime.1 hdiv).isIntegral hpos)
  have PQprim : IsPrimitive (P * Q) := Pmonic.isPrimitive.mul Qmonic.isPrimitive
  have prod : P * Q ∣ X ^ n - 1 := by
    rw [IsPrimitive.Int.dvd_iff_map_cast_dvd_map_cast (P * Q) (X ^ n - 1) PQprim,
      Polynomial.map_mul]
    refine IsCoprime.mul_dvd ?_ ?_ ?_
    · have aux := IsPrimitive.Int.irreducible_iff_irreducible_map_cast Pmonic.isPrimitive
      refine (dvd_or_isCoprime _ _ (aux.1 Pirr)).resolve_left ?_
      rw [map_dvd_map (Int.castRingHom ℚ) Int.cast_injective Pmonic]
      intro hdiv
      refine hdiff (eq_of_monic_of_associated Pmonic Qmonic ?_)
      exact associated_of_dvd_dvd hdiv (Pirr.dvd_symm Qirr hdiv)
    · apply (map_dvd_map (Int.castRingHom ℚ) Int.cast_injective Pmonic).2
      exact minpoly_dvd_x_pow_sub_one h
    · apply (map_dvd_map (Int.castRingHom ℚ) Int.cast_injective Qmonic).2
      exact minpoly_dvd_x_pow_sub_one (pow_of_prime h hprime.1 hdiv)
  replace prod := _root_.map_dvd (mapRingHom (Int.castRingHom (ZMod p))) prod
  rw [coe_mapRingHom, Polynomial.map_mul, Polynomial.map_sub, Polynomial.map_one,
    Polynomial.map_pow, map_X] at prod
  obtain ⟨R, hR⟩ := minpoly_dvd_mod_p h hdiv
  rw [hR, ← mul_assoc, ← Polynomial.map_mul, ← sq, Polynomial.map_pow] at prod
  have habs : map (Int.castRingHom (ZMod p)) P ^ 2 ∣ map (Int.castRingHom (ZMod p)) P ^ 2 * R := by
    use R
  replace habs :=
    lt_of_lt_of_le (Nat.cast_lt.2 one_lt_two)
      (le_emultiplicity_of_pow_dvd (dvd_trans habs prod))
  have hfree : Squarefree (X ^ n - 1 : (ZMod p)[X]) :=
    (separable_X_pow_sub_C 1 (fun h => hdiv <| (ZMod.natCast_eq_zero_iff n p).1 h)
        one_ne_zero).squarefree
  rcases (squarefree_iff_emultiplicity_le_one (X ^ n - 1)).1 hfree
      (map (Int.castRingHom (ZMod p)) P) with hle | hunit
  · rw [Nat.cast_one] at habs; exact hle.not_gt habs
  · replace hunit := degree_eq_zero_of_isUnit hunit
    rw [degree_map_eq_of_leadingCoeff_ne_zero (Int.castRingHom (ZMod p)) _] at hunit
    · exact (minpoly.degree_pos (isIntegral h hpos)).ne' hunit
    simp only [Pmonic, eq_intCast, Monic.leadingCoeff, Int.cast_one, Ne, not_false_iff,
      one_ne_zero]

records.name: Catalan number formula Cₙ=(1/(n+1)) binom(2n,n)
records.statement: For $n\ge0$, the recursively defined Catalan number $C_0=1$, $C_{n+1}=\sum_{i=0}^n C_iC_{n-i}$ satisfies $C_n=\binom{2n}{n}/(n+1)$.
records.proofA:
Write $B_j=\binom{2j}{j}$ and, for $N>0$, set
\[G(N,j)=\frac{B_jB_{N-j}(2j-N)}{2N(N+1)}.\]
The central-binomial recurrence gives, for $0\le i\le d$,
\[G(d+1,i+1)-G(d+1,i)=\frac{B_i}{i+1}\frac{B_{d-i}}{d-i+1}.\]

Induct strongly in the Catalan recurrence and substitute $C_i=B_i/(i+1)$. The resulting convolution telescopes to
\[G(d+1,d+1)-G(d+1,0)=\frac{B_{d+1}}{d+2}.\]
This proves the identity over $\mathbb Q$; divisibility of $B_n$ by $n+1$ gives the natural-number quotient.
records.proofB:
Let $D_n$ be the set of Dyck paths of semilength $n$. First return to height zero gives the disjoint decomposition
\[D_{n+1}\cong\coprod_{i=0}^n D_i\times D_{n-i}.\]
Hence $|D_n|=C_n$ by the Catalan recurrence.

There are $\binom{2n}{n}$ balanced paths. Reflection of the prefix ending at the first step below zero bijects the bad paths with paths having $n+1$ up-steps and $n-1$ down-steps; the inverse reflects through the first visit to height $1$. Thus, for $n\ge1$,
\[C_n=\binom{2n}{n}-\binom{2n}{n-1}=\frac1{n+1}\binom{2n}{n}.\]
The case $n=0$ is immediate.

  sorry

records.name: The sum of reciprocals of the primes diverges
records.statement: The sum of the reciprocals of the prime numbers diverges.
records.proofA: Suppose $\sum_p1/p<\infty$ and choose $y$ with $\sum_{p>y}1/p<1/2$. Among $m\le N$, fewer than $N/2$ have a prime factor exceeding $y$. Each remaining $m$ is a square times a squarefree product of primes at most $y$, so there are at most $2^{\pi(y)}\sqrt N$ such integers. For sufficiently large $N$ this is also $<N/2$, contradicting the count $N$.
records.proofB:
For $P_N=\prod_{p\le N}(1-p^{-1})^{-1}$, unique factorization and the geometric-series expansion give $P_N\ge H_N$. On the other hand,
\[\log P_N=\sum_{p\le N}-\log(1-p^{-1})

records.name: Minkowski inequality for Lᵖ norms
records.statement: For $1\le p<\infty$, the $L^p$ norm satisfies $\|f+g\|_p\le\|f\|_p+\|g\|_p$ whenever $f,g\in L^p$.
records.scope: The linked declaration covers the finite-p nonnegative integral formulation.
records.proofA:
For $1<p<\infty$, set $h=|f+g|$ and $q=p/(p-1)$. Pointwise $h^p\le(|f|+|g|)h^{p-1}$. Hölder's inequality gives
\[\int h^p\le(\|f\|_p+\|g\|_p)\left(\int h^p\right)^{1/q}.\]
The left integral is finite by $h^p\le2^{p-1}(|f|^p+|g|^p)$. If it is nonzero, divide by its $1/q$ power; the zero case is immediate. For $p=1$, integrate the pointwise triangle inequality.
records.proofB:
Put $a=\|f\|_p$ and $b=\|g\|_p$. If either is zero, the result follows from equality almost everywhere. Otherwise set $F=f/a$, $G=g/b$ and $\lambda=a/(a+b)$. Convexity of $z\mapsto|z|^p$ gives
\[|\lambda F+(1-\lambda)G|^p\le\lambda|F|^p+(1-\lambda)|G|^p.\]
After integration, the left side has integral at most $\lambda+(1-\lambda)=1$. Since $f+g=(a+b)(\lambda F+(1-\lambda)G)$, taking $p$th roots yields $\|f+g\|_p\le a+b$.

records.name: Fourier inversion theorem (standard integrable/smooth formulations)
records.statement: Let $f,\widehat f\in L^1(\mathbb R)$, with $\widehat f(\xi)=\int f(t)e^{-2\pi i t\xi}\,dt$. At each continuity point $x$ of $f$, $f(x)=\int\widehat f(\xi)e^{2\pi ix\xi}\,d\xi$.
records.proofA:
For $\varepsilon>0$, insert the cutoff $e^{-\pi\varepsilon^2\xi^2}$ in the inverse Fourier integral. Dominated convergence, using $\widehat f\in L^1$, sends the damped integrals to the inverse Fourier integral. Fubini and the Gaussian Fourier transform identify the same integral with $f*K_\varepsilon$, where
\[K_\varepsilon(t)=\varepsilon^{-1}e^{-\pi t^2/\varepsilon^2}.\]
The $K_\varepsilon$ have unit integral and concentrate at zero. At a continuity point $x$, split the convolution into a neighborhood of zero and its complement; continuity controls the first part and $f\in L^1$ plus Gaussian decay controls the second. Hence $(f*K_\varepsilon)(x)\to f(x)$, and uniqueness of limits proves inversion.
records.proofB:
For $R>0$ put $m_R(\xi)=(1-|\xi|/R)_+$ and
\[K_R(t)=R\left(\frac{\sin(\pi Rt)}{\pi Rt}\right)^2.\]
The triangular multiplier is the Fourier transform of $K_R$; moreover $K_R\ge0$, $\int K_R=1$, and $K_R(t)\le(\pi^2Rt^2)^{-1}$ away from $0$. Fubini gives
\[(f*K_R)(x)=\int\widehat f(\xi)m_R(\xi)e^{2\pi ix\xi}\,d\xi.\]
Dominated convergence sends the right side to the inverse Fourier integral. Splitting the left side near and away from $0$, continuity of $f$ at $x$ and the displayed tail bound give $(f*K_R)(x)\to f(x)$.

records.statement: For $n\ge1$ and positive reals $x_1,\ldots,x_n$, $\frac{x_1+\cdots+x_n}{n}\ge(x_1\cdots x_n)^{1/n}$, with equality exactly when all $x_i$ are equal.
records.proofA:
For $w_i=1/n$, Jensen's inequality for $\exp$ gives
\[\exp\!\left(\frac1n\sum_i\log x_i\right)\le\frac1n\sum_i\exp(\log x_i)=\frac1n\sum_i x_i.\]
The left side is $(\prod_i x_i)^{1/n}$. Strict convexity of $\exp$ gives equality exactly when the $\log x_i$, and hence the $x_i$, are equal.
records.proofB:
Fix $s=\sum_i x_i>0$. The product attains a maximum on the compact simplex $\{y_i\ge0:\sum_i y_i=s\}$. The maximum is positive, since the equal vector has positive product; hence every maximizing coordinate is positive.

If two coordinates $a\ne b$ are replaced by $(a+b)/2$, their sum is unchanged and their product increases by $(a-b)^2/4>0$, a contradiction. Thus the maximum occurs only at $y_i=s/n$, so
\[\prod_i x_i\le(s/n)^n.\]
Taking $n$th roots proves the inequality, with equality exactly when all $x_i=s/n$.

theorem geom_mean_le_arith_mean_weighted (w z : ι → ℝ) (hw : ∀ i ∈ s, 0 ≤ w i)
    (hw' : ∑ i ∈ s, w i = 1) (hz : ∀ i ∈ s, 0 ≤ z i) :
    ∏ i ∈ s, z i ^ w i ≤ ∑ i ∈ s, w i * z i := by
  -- If some number `z i` equals zero and has non-zero weight, then LHS is 0 and RHS is nonnegative.
  by_cases! A : ∃ i ∈ s, z i = 0 ∧ w i ≠ 0
  · rcases A with ⟨i, his, hzi, hwi⟩
    rw [prod_eq_zero his]
    · exact sum_nonneg fun j hj => mul_nonneg (hw j hj) (hz j hj)
    · rw [hzi]
      exact zero_rpow hwi
  -- If all numbers `z i` with non-zero weight are positive, then we apply Jensen's inequality
  -- for `exp` and numbers `log (z i)` with weights `w i`.
  · have := convexOn_exp.map_sum_le hw hw' fun i _ => Set.mem_univ <| log (z i)
    simp only [exp_sum, smul_eq_mul, mul_comm (w _) (log _)] at this
    convert this using 1 <;> [apply prod_congr rfl; apply sum_congr rfl] <;> intro i hi
    · rcases eq_or_lt_of_le (hz i hi) with hz | hz
      · simp [A i hi hz.symm]
      · exact rpow_def_of_pos hz _
    · rcases eq_or_lt_of_le (hz i hi) with hz | hz
      · simp [A i hi hz.symm]
      · rw [exp_log hz]

theorem geom_mean_eq_arith_mean_weighted_iff_of_pos' (w z : ι → ℝ) (hw : ∀ i ∈ s, 0 < w i)
    (hw' : ∑ i ∈ s, w i = 1) (hz : ∀ i ∈ s, 0 ≤ z i) :
    ∏ i ∈ s, z i ^ w i = ∑ i ∈ s, w i * z i ↔ ∀ j ∈ s, z j = ∑ i ∈ s, w i * z i := by
  by_cases! A : ∃ i ∈ s, z i = 0 ∧ w i ≠ 0
  · rcases A with ⟨i, his, hzi, hwi⟩
    rw [prod_eq_zero his]
    · constructor
      · intro h
        rw [← h]
        intro j hj
        apply eq_zero_of_ne_zero_of_mul_left_eq_zero (ne_of_lt (hw j hj)).symm
        apply (sum_eq_zero_iff_of_nonneg ?_).mp h.symm j hj
        exact fun i hi => (mul_nonneg_iff_of_pos_left (hw i hi)).mpr (hz i hi)
      · intro h
        convert h i his
        exact hzi.symm
    · rw [hzi]
      exact zero_rpow hwi
  · have hz' := fun i h => lt_of_le_of_ne (hz i h) (fun a => (ne_of_gt (hw i h)) (A i h a.symm))
    have := strictConvexOn_exp.map_sum_eq_iff hw hw' fun i _ => Set.mem_univ <| log (z i)
    simp only [exp_sum, smul_eq_mul, mul_comm (w _) (log _)] at this
    convert this using 1
    · apply Eq.congr <;>
      [apply prod_congr rfl; apply sum_congr rfl] <;>
      intro i hi <;>
      simp only [exp_mul, exp_log (hz' i hi)]
    · constructor <;> intro h j hj
      · rw [← arith_mean_weighted_of_constant s w _ (log (z j)) hw' fun i _ => congrFun rfl]
        apply sum_congr rfl
        intro x hx
        simp only [mul_comm, h j hj, h x hx]
      · rw [← arith_mean_weighted_of_constant s w _ (z j) hw' fun i _ => congrFun rfl]
        apply sum_congr rfl
        intro x hx
        simp only [log_injOn_pos (hz' j hj) (hz' x hx), h j hj, h x hx]
